detail.extracted_title: Geometry, Spirit, and the Reed Pen: Omani Calligrapher Ahmed Al-Muraikhi and Global Masters on the Living Art of the Arabic Letter
detail.excerpt: From Muscat's architectural installations to studios in Shandong, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, Istanbul, and Herat, master calligraphers examine how the Arabic script crosses linguistic borders while guarding its classical proportions and legibility.
detail.article_html:
When an observer who does not speak a word of Arabic stands before a panel of Thuluth or geometric Kufic script, the eye still registers rhythm, tension, and architectural balance. Measured by circular dot units (nuqadd) established over a millennium ago, Arabic calligraphy has long traveled far beyond its geographic birthplace. In an international cultural investigation by journalist Faisal bin Said Al-Alawi, Omani calligrapher Ahmed Al-Muraikhi joins practitioners from China, Malaysia, Indonesia, Turkey, Afghanistan, Egypt, and Syria to examine a central artistic question: how can the Arabic letter embrace contemporary media and diverse cultural aesthetics without losing its soul or legibility?

Ahmed Al-Muraikhi: Renewing the Medium While Protecting the Proportion

For Omani calligrapher Ahmed Al-Muraikhi, the Arabic letter sits at the intersection of identity, spiritual presence, and semantic meaning. Looking at his own horizontal Kufic composition of Verse 261 from Surah Al-Baqarah—"like a grain that sprouts seven ears; in every ear a hundred grains"—Al-Muraikhi argues that genuine artistic renewal belongs in the choice of tools, surfaces, and spatial presentation rather than the destruction of classical letter anatomy.

In Al-Muraikhi's view, contemporary calligraphers have wide latitude to move beyond traditional soot ink and handmade paper into forged iron, sculpted light, digital motion, three-dimensional installation, and public architecture. Yet he draws a firm boundary around the structural proportions (nisbah) of the script and the readability of the text—particularly when inscribing Quranic verses. Stripping the letter of its linguistic meaning and reducing it to an indecipherable graphic shape, he cautions, severs the bond between eye and intellect, turning a living communicative art into mute ornament.

From Chinese Ink Brushwork to Southeast Asian Jawi Heritage

Across East and Southeast Asia, master calligraphers have spent centuries conversing with the Arabic alphabet through their own regional instruments and historical memories:

  • Haji Noor Deen Mi Guangjiang (China): Trained initially in historic Chinese mosques before studying in Kuwait and Egypt and earning his formal calligraphic licence (Ijazah) in Turkey, Haji Noor Deen merges canonical Thuluth and Naskh rules with the fluid velocity of traditional Chinese horsehair brushes and rice paper. Rather than abandoning classical Arabic measurement, his Sini-inspired compositions allow two ancient calligraphic traditions to inhabit a single stroke.
  • Abdul Baki bin Abu Bakar (Malaysia): Tracing the Malay Archipelago's relationship with Arabic script back to the early fourteenth-century Terengganu Inscription Stone, Abdul Baki explains how the Jawi alphabet served for centuries as the primary vehicle for Malay literature, law, and scholarship. Although British colonial administration replaced Jawi with the Latin alphabet in daily governance, continuous engagement with Quranic Naskh preserved local reverence for the script, inspiring young Malaysian calligraphers who today train across Kuala Lumpur, Iraq, and Istanbul.
  • Ahmad Jalaluddin (Indonesia): Inside Indonesia's traditional Islamic boarding schools (pesantren), students learn calligraphy alongside Quranic exegesis (tafsir). Jalaluddin notes that before an Indonesian calligrapher touches reed to paper, the artist studies the meaning and emotional cadence of the verse or Hadith so that visual composition serves comprehension.

A Thousand Years of Architectural Script and Classical Discipline

Further north and west, calligraphers in Turkey, Afghanistan, Egypt, and Syria emphasize that creative freedom only endures when anchored in rigorous apprenticeship:

  • Murat Kurt (Turkey): Highlighting that Turkish speakers wrote their language in the Arabic alphabet for nearly a thousand years—from the mystical poetry of Yunus Emre and Fuzuli to the stone portals of Seljuk and Ottoman mosques—Kurt maintains that each generation must contribute a fresh visual sensibility rather than mechanically copying nineteenth-century plates.
  • Mohammad Younus Jami (Afghanistan): Specializing in Mushafi Kufic and classical illumination (Tazhib), Jami describes geometric calligraphy as a vessel of inner stillness (sakinah) and cross-cultural dialogue, where mathematical discipline transcends spoken vernaculars.
  • Khalifa Al-Shimi (Egypt) and Bilal Basmaji (Syria): Addressing the rapid spread of Arabic typography across global fashion, commercial branding, and contemporary art galleries, both masters stress that experimentation succeeds only after an artist has internalised classical rules.

Whether carved into the stone friezes of Muscat, brushed onto absorbent paper in eastern China, or illuminated in Herat, the consensus among these masters remains remarkably unified: the Arabic letter thrives globally precisely because its geometric laws keep form and meaning inseparable.

detail.instagram_caption:
How does the Arabic letter cross linguistic and geographical borders—from Muscat to Shandong, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, Istanbul, and Herat—while preserving its classical geometric proportions and legibility?

In an international cultural investigation by Faisal bin Said Al-Alawi in Oman Daily, Omani calligrapher Ahmed Al-Muraikhi joins master calligraphers across Asia and the Middle East to examine the balance between heritage and contemporary experimentation.

For Al-Muraikhi, renewal belongs in materials and spatial presentation—expanding from ink and paper into iron, light, digital media, three-dimensional space, and architecture—while keeping the letter's foundational proportions and semantic clarity intact, particularly when inscribing Quranic verses.

Across Asia, Chinese master Haji Noor Deen merges canonical Thuluth and Naskh rules with traditional Chinese brushwork; Malaysian calligrapher Abdul Baki bin Abu Bakar traces the Jawi script back to the fourteenth-century Terengganu Inscription Stone; Indonesian calligrapher Ahmad Jalaluddin links script practice inside Islamic institutes to Quranic exegesis; and Turkish and Afghan masters Murat Kurt and Mohammad Younus Jami reflect on a millennium of architectural Kufic and classical discipline.

Read the full analysis at omanspire.om (link in bio).
